title: A Tale of Two Domains: Exploring Efficient Architecture Design for Truly Autonomous Things
problem: Autonomous Things require simultaneous optimization of energy autonomy and inference autonomy, but existing designs typically address only one domain independently. Practical AuT systems need tailored architectures with significantly improved inference performance and more efficient energy utilization across both domains.
motivation: AuT enables ubiquitous deployment of intelligent computation on emerging consumer electronics and mission-critical infrastructures.
method: CHRYSALIS automatically designs hardware for autonomous devices by combining three elements: a model of energy harvesting and intermittent operation (when the device shuts down due to low power) plus accelerator control; a tool that searches for the best hardware designs within size, weight, and power constraints; and a system model showing how energy and processing choices affect each other. Unlike traditional approaches that optimize these separately, it treats energy efficiency and processing performance as linked challenges that must be solved together.
key_novelty: The core innovation is treating energy efficiency and processing performance as a single co-design problem rather than as two separate optimization challenges.
contributions: CHRYSALIS automated methodology for energy autonomy and inference autonomy co-design in AuT systems
Architectural modeling framework encompassing energy harvesting, intermittent execution, and accelerator control
Intelligent architecture generation tool for SWaP-constrained design space exploration
Validation demonstrating 56.4% average performance improvement over state-of-the-art AuT designs
